paragraphs: In inquiries of every kind there are certain primary truths, or first principles, on which all later reasoning depends. Such truths carry an internal evidence that wins the mind's assent before any reflection or combining of ideas. When they fail to do so, the cause must lie either in some defect or disorder of the organs of perception, or in the pull of some strong interest, passion or prejudice. The maxims of geometry are of this kind: "the whole is greater than its part; things equal to the same are equal to one another; two straight lines cannot enclose a space; and all right angles are equal to each other." So are these other maxims of ethics and politics: that there cannot be an effect without a cause; that the means ought to be proportioned to the end; that every power ought to be commensurate with its object; that there ought to be no limitation of a power destined to effect a purpose which is itself incapable of limitation. And these two latter sciences contain other truths which, though they cannot claim to rank as axioms, are such direct inferences from axioms, are so obvious in themselves, and agree so well with the natural, unsophisticated dictates of common sense, that they win the assent of a sound and unbiased mind with almost equally irresistible force and conviction.

The objects of geometrical inquiry stand so far removed from the pursuits that stir up the unruly passions of the human heart that people accept without difficulty not only the simpler theorems of the science but even those abstruse paradoxes which, although they may seem capable of demonstration, run against the natural conceptions the mind would form on the subject without the aid of philosophy. The INFINITE DIVISIBILITY of matter, in other words the INFINITE divisibility of a FINITE thing, extending down to the smallest atom, is a point agreed among geometricians. It is no less incomprehensible to common sense than any of those mysteries in religion against which the batteries of infidelity have been so industriously aimed.

In the sciences of morals and politics, however, men are far less easily led. To a certain degree it is right and useful that they should be so, because caution and investigation are a necessary armor against error and imposition. But this resistance can be carried too far, and can degenerate into obstinacy, perverseness or dishonesty. It cannot be claimed that the principles of moral and political knowledge have, in general, the same certainty as those of mathematics. Yet they have much better claims to certainty than the conduct of men in particular situations would lead us to grant. The obscurity lies much more often in the passions and prejudices of the reasoner than in the subject. Too often men do not give their own understandings a fair chance. They yield to some unfortunate bias, and they entangle themselves in words and confound themselves in subtleties.

How else could it happen (if we grant that the objectors are sincere) that positions as clear as those showing the necessity of a general power of taxation in the government of the Union should find any opponents among men of discernment? These positions have been fully stated elsewhere. Still, it may not be improper to restate them here, as an introduction to examining whatever has been offered against them. In substance they are as follows:

A government ought to contain within itself every power needed to accomplish fully the objects committed to its care and to carry out completely the trusts for which it is responsible. It ought to be free of every other control except a regard for the public good and for the sense of the people.

Overseeing the national defense and securing the public peace against foreign or domestic violence involve providing for emergencies and dangers to which no possible limits can be set. The power to make that provision, therefore, ought to know no bounds other than the necessities of the nation and the resources of the community.

Revenue is the essential engine by which the means of meeting the national necessities must be obtained. The power to obtain revenue in its full extent must therefore be included in the power to provide for those necessities.

Theory and practice both show that the power to raise revenue is ineffective when it is exercised over the States in their collective capacities. The federal government must therefore of necessity be given an unqualified power of taxation in the ordinary modes.

If experience did not show otherwise, it would be natural to conclude that the propriety of a general power of taxation in the national government could safely rest on the evidence of these propositions, without further arguments or illustrations. But in fact we find that the opponents of the proposed Constitution, far from accepting the justness or truth of these propositions, seem to direct their principal and most zealous effort against this very part of the plan. It may therefore be satisfactory to analyze the arguments they use against it.

The arguments they have labored over most for this purpose seem in substance to come to this: "It is not true that, because the necessities of the Union may not be capable of limitation, its power of laying taxes ought to be unconfined. Revenue is as necessary for the purposes of the local administrations as for those of the Union, and the former are at least as important as the latter to the happiness of the people. It is therefore as necessary that the State governments should be able to command the means of supplying their wants as that the national government should have the same ability for the wants of the Union. But an indefinite power of taxation in the LATTER might, and probably would in time, deprive the FORMER of the means of providing for their own necessities, and would put them entirely at the mercy of the national legislature. The laws of the Union are to become the supreme law of the land, and the Union is to have power to pass all laws that may be NECESSARY for carrying into execution the authorities with which it is proposed to vest it. The national government might therefore abolish at any time the taxes imposed for State objects, on the pretense that they interfere with its own. It might claim that this was necessary in order to give effect to the national revenues. And thus all the resources of taxation might by degrees become the subjects of federal monopoly, to the entire exclusion and destruction of the State governments."

At times this reasoning seems to rest on the supposition that the national government will usurp power. At other times it seems intended only as a deduction from the constitutional operation of its intended powers. Only in the latter light can it claim any fairness. The moment we launch into conjectures about usurpations by the federal government, we plunge into an unfathomable abyss and place ourselves entirely beyond the reach of reasoning. Imagination may roam at will until it is bewildered among the labyrinths of an enchanted castle, and cannot tell which way to turn to get out of the perplexities it has so rashly entered. Whatever the limits or modifications of the Union's powers, it is easy to imagine an endless train of possible dangers. By indulging an excess of jealousy and timidity, we may bring ourselves to a state of absolute skepticism and irresolution. I repeat here what I have said in substance elsewhere: every observation founded on the danger of usurpation ought to be directed to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers. The State governments, by their original constitutions, are invested with complete sovereignty. What does our security against usurpation from that quarter consist in? Doubtless in the manner of their formation, and in the proper dependence of those who are to administer them on the people. If the proposed structure of the federal government turns out, on impartial examination, to give the same kind of security to a proper extent, then all apprehensions about usurpation ought to be discarded.

We should not forget that the State governments are quite as likely to be disposed to encroach on the rights of the Union as the Union is to encroach on the rights of the State governments. Which side would prevail in such a conflict must depend on the means the contending parties could use to secure success. In republics strength is always on the side of the people, and there are weighty reasons to believe that the State governments will commonly have the most influence over them. The natural conclusion is that such contests will most often end to the disadvantage of the Union, and that the members are more likely to encroach on the federal head than the federal head on the members. But all conjectures of this kind must plainly be extremely vague and fallible. By far the safest course is to set them entirely aside and to confine our attention wholly to the nature and extent of the powers as the Constitution lays them out. Everything beyond this must be left to the prudence and firmness of the people. They will hold the scales in their own hands, and it is to be hoped they will always take care to preserve the constitutional equilibrium between the general and the State governments. On this ground, which is evidently the true one, it will not be difficult to answer the objections that have been made to an indefinite power of taxation in the United States.
